title: Why Two People Never Book the Same Seat on BookMyShow at Once — Engineering Cheat Sheet
subtitle: Achieving strict concurrency control via distributed locking and atomic database transactions.
summary: This architectural challenge centers on preventing race conditions in high-concurrency seat selection systems. By leveraging pessimistic locking or transactional isolation, platforms ensure data consistency across distributed nodes without compromising system throughput.

key_concepts.name: Pessimistic Locking
key_concepts.detail: Uses 'SELECT ... FOR UPDATE' in SQL to lock database rows at the start of a transaction, preventing other processes from modifying or acquiring the same record.

key_concepts.name: Optimistic Concurrency Control
key_concepts.detail: Uses versioning or timestamps; a transaction succeeds only if the seat status remains unchanged since the initial read, failing gracefully if a conflict occurs during commit.

key_concepts.name: Distributed Locking (Redis)
key_concepts.detail: Uses Redlock or similar patterns to acquire a time-bound lease on a seat ID across distributed application servers, ensuring cross-instance synchronization before hitting the DB.

code_cheatsheet.explanation: Atomically acquires a lock on seat 123 for 30 seconds only if it doesn't exist (NX), preventing race conditions before DB persistence.

code_cheatsheet.code: db.session.execute('SELECT * FROM seats WHERE id = :id FOR UPDATE', {'id': 123})
code_cheatsheet.explanation: Executes a blocking row-level lock within a transaction, forcing other threads to wait until the current booking request commits or rolls back.

best_practices: Prefer database-level row locks for strict integrity, shifting to distributed caches only when throughput exceeds RDBMS capabilities.
Implement short TTLs (Time-To-Live) on locks to prevent orphaned resources if an application service crashes mid-transaction.
Use idempotent APIs to handle client retries without creating duplicate bookings or corrupted seat states.
Maintain high observability by tracking lock contention metrics and average latency of the critical booking write path.

interview_qa.question: How do you prevent overbooking when thousands of users hit a single seat simultaneously?
interview_qa.answer: Use strict serializable isolation levels or pessimistic row-level locking at the database layer to ensure atomicity. To scale, implement a 'Seat Reservation' cache with Redis, where the seat status moves from 'Available' to 'Held' via atomic operations before the final persistent write occurs.
